ui.statique.texte: {marque} is a free daily game: three picture puzzles about the world's dishes, monuments, festivals, traditions and objects, each to match with its country. No account, just a few minutes.

ui.regles.jour: One challenge a day, the same for everyone. It changes at midnight, your device's time.
ui.regles.semaine: The week gets harder as it goes: easy on Monday and Tuesday, hard on Saturday, and a big challenge on Sunday.
ui.regles.origine: Where's it from? Four clues to find the country: a detail of the photo (100 points), the whole photo (70), the name (40), then a choice of four countries (20). After each mistake, the game tells you whether you're on the right continent.
ui.regles.intrus: Odd One Out. Three curiosities come from the same country, the fourth from another country on the same continent. 100 points on the first try, 50 on the second.
ui.regles.liens: Matchups. Four curiosities, five countries, so one country too many. 100 points for four correct matches, 70 for three, 45 for two, 20 for one.
ui.regles.serie: Playing every day builds your streak. Once you've played two days in a row, one missed day is forgiven, once every seven days.
ui.regles.rattachement: A curiosity belongs to the country where it was born or with which it is most associated. The expected answer is the one in the Wikipedia article shown after each round.
ui.regles.couverture: The game covers {pays} countries and {curiosites} curiosities. Spotted a mistake? Every answer links to its source.
ui.langue.texte: The game is available in several languages. Your progress is the same in all of them.
ui.sauvegarde.texte: No account: your streak, atlas and album stay on this device. To switch phones or avoid losing them, keep this code.

ui.sauvegarde.rappel: Your progress only exists on this device. Keep your backup code so you don't lose it.

ducasse-mons.fait: It is often called the “Doudou,” after a traditional tune played during the festival, which takes place every year on Trinity weekend.

dougga.fait: UNESCO sees it as the “best-preserved small Roman town in North Africa”; the site covers 75 hectares, in the middle of the countryside.

bardo.fait: Housed since 1888 in a former beylical palace in Tunis, this museum holds one of the largest collections of Roman mosaics in the world.

lablabi.fait: This popular dish made with chickpeas, garlic, cumin or caraway and harissa takes its name from the Turkish leblebi, meaning “roasted chickpeas.”

harissa.fait: This red chili paste originated in Tunisia; the know-how associated with it has been on the Intangible Cultural Heritage list since 2022.

machmoum.fait: This bouquet of flowers is made in Tunisia from jasmine, through several stages of production.

mezoued.fait: This traditional North African wind instrument, widespread mainly in Tunisia, gave its name to a form of Tunisian popular music.

bambalouni.fait: This sweet ring-shaped doughnut, fried in oil, is eaten sprinkled with sugar, ideally in the afternoon around snack time.

poterie-sejnane.fait: Passed down from grandmother to granddaughter, this craft relies on entirely manual shaping, without a wheel, and on natural materials.

karnak.fait: Developed over more than 2,000 years by successive pharaohs, this complex covers more than 2 km²; it is the largest religious complex of antiquity.

temple-louxor.fait: Dedicated to the worship of Amun and built mostly under the 18th and 19th Dynasties, this temple was partly turned into a military camp in Roman times.

pyramide-djeser.fait: Designed by the architect Imhotep at Saqqara, this royal tomb was the first to take the shape of a pyramid.

colosses-memnon.fait: These two monumental statues are the last remains of the temple of Amenhotep III; one of them cracked during an earthquake in 27 BC.

temple-hatchepsout.fait: Built entirely of limestone, this temple at Deir el-Bahari replaces pylons with porticoes at the entrance to each terrace.

canal-suez.fait: Dug between 1859 and 1869 under the direction of Ferdinand de Lesseps, it is 193.3 km long and spares ships from sailing around Africa.

masque-toutankhamon.fait: This gold mask was discovered on October 28, 1925, when the British archaeologist Howard Carter opened the pharaoh's sarcophagus.

papyrus.fait: This writing material made from the stems of a plant is an Egyptian invention about 5,000 years old, used until the 11th century.

vase-canope.fait: In ancient Egypt, these jars, four in number, held the embalmed organs of the deceased and were placed near the sarcophagus.

barque-solaire.fait: Found dismantled in 1954 in a pit at the foot of the pyramid, this twenty-ton boat is made of cedar of Lebanon.

senet.fait: This board game, the most widely played among the ancient Egyptians of the New Kingdom, has existed since the Predynastic period.

leptis-magna.fait: This city was one of the important towns of the Carthaginian Republic before coming under the authority of Rome at the end of the Third Punic War.

sabratha.fait: In antiquity, this city formed, with Oea and Leptis Magna, the trio of cities that gave Tripolitania its name.

cyrene.fait: This city was the oldest and most important of the five Greek colonies of Cyrenaica, a region of which it was the capital.

ghadames.fait: Nicknamed the “Pearl of the Desert,” this oasis is one of the earliest fortified towns of the Sahara; its architecture is designed to withstand the extreme climate.

tadrart-acacus.fait: This massif in the southwest of the country holds a major collection of rock art depicting people, animals, horses and later dromedaries.

waw-an-namus.fait: Its name means “oasis of mosquitoes”: this Saharan caldera contains a volcanic cone and small lakes.

chinguetti.fait: This town in the Adrar is cut in two by a dry wadi: on one side the old town, which is gradually being buried by sand, on the other the new one.

ouadane.fait: This town in the Adrar region, northeast of Chinguetti, has an old town listed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

oualata.fait: Like those of Ouadane, Chinguetti and Tichitt, the fortified village of this southeastern town has been a World Heritage Site since 1996.

richat.fait: This circular structure about 50 km in diameter can only be fully seen from space; it is now seen as the remains of a giant collapsed volcano.

banc-arguin.fait: Established in 1976, this 12,000 km² park, shared between the Atlantic Ocean and the Sahara Desert, covers a third of the country's coastline.

mosquee-bleue.fait: Built between 1609 and 1616 in Istanbul, it owes its name to the mainly blue tiles of its interior walls and has six minarets.

topkapi.fait: The residence of the Ottoman sultans from 1465 to 1853, this Istanbul palace bears a name meaning “Cannon Gate Palace.”

grand-bazar.fait: Opened in 1455, this covered market in Istanbul has 65 indoor streets and nearly 4,000 shops.

tour-galata.fait: This cylindrical medieval structure overlooks an Istanbul district north of the Golden Horn and houses a museum.

celsus.fait: Built between 117 and 125 in Ephesus, this Roman public library also served as a mausoleum for the senator whose name it bears.

gobekli-tepe.fait: Occupied from about 9300 to 7500 BC, this prehistoric site is known for its carved T-shaped pillars, which represent stylized humans.

troie.fait: This ancient city, at the center of the stories of the Iliad, is now located on the hill of Hisarlik, at the entrance to the Hellespont.

loukoum.fait: This confection, born in the Ottoman Empire, is a paste of starch and flavored sugar, dusted with powdered sugar and sometimes filled with nuts.

doner.fait: Born in the 19th century in Bursa, this dish takes its name from the Turkish verb dönmek, “to turn”: the meat cooks on a vertical spit that rotates on itself.

raki.fait: This anise-flavored grape brandy is the country's national drink; its name derives from the Arabic araq.

simit.fait: This circular bread with sesame seeds is often sold on the street by vendors who carry it on a cart or on their heads.

dondurma.fait: This beaten ice cream contains salep and mastic; it is said to come from the city of Maraş, whose name it sometimes bears.

karagoz.fait: This shadow theater bears the name of its hero, an illiterate common man whose name means “black eye,” facing the learned Hacivat.

iznik.fait: Produced from the mid-15th century in the town of İznik, ancient Nicaea, this pottery was long called “Rhodes ware.”

persepolis.fait: Founded in 521 BC by order of Darius I, this capital of the Achaemenid Persian Empire was partly destroyed by Alexander the Great.

naghch-e-djahan.fait: Built in the early 17th century by Shah Abbas I in Isfahan, this square measuring 560 by 160 meters is one of the largest in the world.

si-o-se-pol.fait: Its name means “bridge of thirty-three arches”: built around 1608 in Isfahan, this two-level bridge also serves as a dam on the river.

badgir.fait: Its Persian name means “wind catcher”: this element of traditional architecture creates natural ventilation in buildings.

arg-e-bam.fait: This citadel city on the Silk Road is the largest adobe complex in the world; an earthquake almost completely destroyed it in 2003.

palais-golestan.fait: This former royal palace of the Qajar dynasty is in Tehran; its Persian name means “palace of the flower garden.”

tchelo-kabab.fait: Considered the national dish, it combines steamed rice with a kebab; it was probably created under the Qajar dynasty.

faloodeh.fait: This frozen dessert made with rice vermicelli, lemon juice and rosewater was originally prepared in the Shiraz region.

gabbeh.fait: This small rug with a very thick pile is hand-knotted, almost exclusively by women of nomadic tribes; its Persian name means “raw.”

ziggourat-ur.fait: Built at the beginning of the 21st century BC, it is one of the best-preserved ziggurats in Mesopotamia; its remains were excavated in the 1920s and 1930s.

babylone.fait: This ancient city on the banks of the Euphrates reached its peak in the 6th century BC; its ziggurat may have inspired the myth of the Tower of Babel.

samarra.fait: This spiral minaret belongs to a 9th-century mosque that was for centuries the largest in Islamic civilization.

hatra.fait: The capital of a kingdom allied with the Parthian Empire, this city flourished mainly in the 2nd century and withstood several sieges by the armies of the Roman Empire.

citadelle-erbil.fait: The oldest traces of occupation of this tell date back at least to the 5th millennium BC; it rises 25 to 32 meters above the plain.

mudhif.fait: This large ceremonial reed house is built by the Marsh Arabs in the south of the country; a local sheikh pays for it and maintains it for his guests.

samoon.fait: This yeast bread baked in traditional stone ovens is one of the most popular in the country; yogurt with live cultures often serves as its starter.

baalbek.fait: The Romans left three giant temples there, including that of Bacchus, one of the best preserved in the Greco-Roman world.

jeita.fait: This system of two caves can be visited by boat in its lower part; the largest chamber reaches 120 meters in height.

byblos.fait: The Greeks gave it this name because papyrus, búblos in Ancient Greek, was imported into Greece from this city, which is said to have been founded around 5000 BC.

cedres-dieu.fait: This forest is one of the last remnants of the ancient cedar forest of Mount Lebanon; it has been a World Heritage Site since 1998.

raouche.fait: These two limestone islets washed by the Mediterranean rise off the Corniche of Beirut; the site is also called the Pigeons' Grotto.

palmyre.fait: This ancient city stood near a desert oasis, 210 km northeast of Damascus; the site has been a World Heritage Site since 1980.

krak-chevaliers.fait: The Knights Hospitaller held this castle from 1142 to 1271, when it was conquered by Sultan Baybars after 129 years of invincibility.

omeyyades.fait: This great mosque was built in Damascus between 706 and 715 by the Umayyad caliph Al-Walid I.

citadelle-alep.fait: This fortified medieval palace, built on a tell overlooking the city center, is recognizable by its imposing fortified entrance.

savon-alep.fait: This soap is made from olive oil and contains laurel berry oil; it bears the name of its city of origin.

piment-alep.fait: Its pods turn burgundy as they ripen, then are semi-dried, seeded and crushed; it owes its name to a city on the Silk Road.

hegra.fait: Nicknamed the second Petra for its rock-cut tombs, this Nabataean site became in 2008 the country's first World Heritage Site.

kaaba.fait: Its Arabic name means “the cube”: this building covered with black silk cloth is the holiest site in Islam.

masjid-nabawi.fait: The original mosque, built by Muhammad in Medina, was only a small part of the present building, enlarged by the caliphs and then by the kingdom.

kabsa.fait: This dish of rice and mutton or chicken is seasoned with a blend of spices: cumin, coriander, cinnamon, cardamom, cloves and dried lime.

socotra.fait: This island in the Arabian Sea, 133 kilometers long, is home to some 700 species found nowhere else in the world.

dar-al-hajar.fait: Built in the 1920s on a 50 m high rock, this palace near Sanaa was the summer residence of Imam Yahya.

janbiya.fait: This dagger with a short, curved blade is worn on the belt with traditional clothing; it tends to be more a symbol than a weapon.

zabid.fait: One of the oldest cities in the country, it was its capital between the 13th and 15th centuries; its university was then prestigious.

saltah.fait: This meat stew topped with fenugreek froth is often eaten with flatbread, which serves as a spoon to scoop up the food.

massada.fait: These ancient palaces and fortifications, built by Herod the Great, are perched on top of an isolated mountain in the Judaean Desert.

ville-blanche.fait: This ensemble forms the center of the new city of Tel Aviv; UNESCO added it to the World Heritage List in 2003.

makhtesh-ramon.fait: This erosion cirque in the Negev Desert is 40 km long and 500 m deep; its Hebrew name means “the Ramon crater.”

cesaree.fait: This ancient city on the Mediterranean coast preserves the ruins of Herod the Great's royal capital and many Roman and medieval monuments.

garni.fait: The only surviving Hellenistic Greek temple in the country, it collapsed in the earthquake of 1679 and was rebuilt between 1969 and 1975.

khatchkar.fait: Its name means “cross stone”: this stele carved with one or more crosses is generally 1.5 to 2 m high.

lac-sevan.fait: The country's largest lake, this “true inland sea” covers 1,400 km², two and a half times the size of Lake Geneva.

tatev.fait: This monastery in the Goris region, 316 km from Yerevan, is the most important monument in the south of the country.

khor-virap.fait: This monastery is in the Ararat region, not far from the capital Yerevan; it is overlooked by Mount Ararat.

vardavar.fait: During this traditional festival, also called Vartavar, people of all ages drench one another with water.

khorovats.fait: This barbecued meat skewer, made with lamb, pork, beef or chicken, is usually reserved for festive occasions.

chirvanchahs.fait: Built in Baku in the 15th century, this palace of the rulers of Shirvan includes a mosque from 1441, baths and a mausoleum.

gobustan.fait: About 65 km from Baku, this reserve holds some 6,000 rock drawings 5,000 to 20,000 years old, as well as mud volcanoes.

ateshgah.fait: This temple of fire worshippers, now an open-air museum, is located on the Absheron Peninsula, 30 km from the center of Baku.

palais-chaki.fait: Built in 1797 by Muhammad Hasan Khan, this palace was the summer residence of the khans of Shaki.

mugham.fait: This classical musical genre gives a leading role to improvisation; it combines singing with the tar, an 11-string lute, and the kamancheh, a bowed fiddle.

chekerboura.fait: This sweet pastry, popular in the country, is eaten in Baku in particular during the Novruz holiday.

khinkali.fait: This dumpling, most often filled with meat, contains broth: you hold it in your hands, bite into the dough and suck out the broth.

tchourtchkhela.fait: This traditional confection consists mainly of grape juice, nuts and flour; it is listed as part of the country's intangible cultural heritage.

vardzia.fait: This 12th-century cave monastery complex was surrounded by a network of fortresses, to serve as a stronghold in case of attack from the south.

ouplistsikhe.fait: This rock-hewn town near Gori brings together structures ranging from the Iron Age to the late Middle Ages, where pagan and Christian architecture stand side by side.

supra.fait: This meal is also a ritual of community gathering; there are two types, one to celebrate a festive occasion, the other to mark a time of mourning.

panduri.fait: This three-stringed instrument, once reserved for nobles, symbolizes joy; it may not be played when someone has died.

katskhi.fait: This limestone monolith about forty meters high has a 9th- or 10th-century hermitage on its summit; researchers did not climb it until 1944.

tkemali.fait: This name refers both to a variety of plum from the country and to the plum sauce of which it is the main ingredient.

tchonguri.fait: This four-stringed instrument is played in the west of the country, in the regions of Mingrelia, Guria and Adjara.

gour-emir.fait: This mausoleum in Samarkand is the burial place of Tamerlane, also called Timur the Lame, and of his descendants.

bibi-khanym.fait: Built from 1399 to 1404 in Samarkand, it is said, according to the chronicles, to have required five hundred workers and ninety-five Indian elephants.

samanides.fait: Built around 900 in Bukhara, this mausoleum made entirely of brick bears decoration that imitates the weave of basketry.

tchor-minor.fait: Its Persian name means “four minarets”; this Bukhara building was constructed in 1807 with funds from a wealthy Turkmen merchant.

minaret-jam.fait: Standing 65 meters tall, this slender minaret dates from the late 12th or early 13th century and rises along the Hari Rud river.

band-e-amir.fait: Their name means “dam of the emir” in Dari: these six lakes lie in the heart of the Hindu Kush mountains.

bouzkachi.fait: This collective equestrian activity, whose Persian name means “goat-grabbing game,” is the national sport in Afghanistan.

citadelle-herat.fait: Also called the Citadel of Alexander, this fortress founded by Alexander the Great has been destroyed and rebuilt many times.

jardins-babur.fait: Located southeast of Kabul, this historic park is one of the oldest Mughal gardens to have survived to the present day.

kabuli-palaw.fait: This pilaf combines steamed rice, carrots, caramelized raisins and marinated lamb; it is traditionally garnished with almonds and pistachios.

braai.fait: This Afrikaner barbecue is above all a social custom; “braai vleis” means “grilled meat” in Afrikaans.

bobotie.fait: This dish made with ground meat, chutney, raisins and spices has a topping of egg and milk-soaked bread; it is browned in the oven.

rooibos.fait: Its Afrikaans name means “reddish bush”; its oxidized leaves make a caffeine-free infusion, traditionally served with milk.

cap-bonne-esperance.fait: This rocky headland is not the southernmost point of Africa: that title goes to Cape Agulhas, 149 km to the east-southeast.

parc-kruger.fait: The largest wildlife reserve in South Africa, this park covers nearly 20,000 km², a size comparable to that of Slovenia.

yassa.fait: In this dish, meat or fish is marinated in lemon juice and spices, then fried and simmered in an onion sauce.

pont-faidherbe.fait: This bridge is the only crossing to the historic island of Saint-Louis; it is named after General Louis Faidherbe.

djoudj.fait: This national park, located about sixty kilometers north of Saint-Louis, is a paradise for migratory birds.

cafe-touba.fait: This coffee is flavored with Guinea pepper, a spice ground and mixed with the coffee, then prepared using the classic drip coffee method.

djingareyber.fait: Built between 1325 and 1327 in Timbuktu, it takes its name from Songhay: “jingaray,” mosque, and “beer,” great.

ciwara.fait: This ritual crest mask from Bambara culture has the shape of a roan antelope; its name means “head of the wild beast of farming.”

sanke-mon.fait: This collective fishing rite takes place in a pond in the town of San, on the second Thursday of the seventh lunar month, to commemorate its founding.

mosquee-mopti.fait: Often called the Komoguel Mosque, it is the main place of worship in the town of Mopti, in Mali.

kakum.fait: In this tropical rainforest national park, walkways cross the canopy at a height of about forty meters.

homowo.fait: The name of this festival of the Ga people means “to mock hunger”: it recalls a famine that occurred in precolonial times.

lucy.fait: This 3.18-million-year-old australopithecine fossil, 40% complete, was discovered in 1974 at the Hadar site.

lac-nakuru.fait: This soda lake in the Great Rift Valley is protected by a national park and designated a Ramsar site for the importance of its wetland.

nyama-choma.fait: This grilled goat meat is considered the national dish of Kenya; its name means “barbecue meat” in Kiswahili.

matatu.fait: The name of these minibuses, often painted with graffiti, comes from “tatu,” “three” in Swahili, in reference to the former fare.

lac-natron.fait: This soda lake takes its name from natron, a mineral one of whose components is dissolved in its waters; they attract a large community of lesser flamingos.

olduvai.fait: This gorge has yielded stone tools and fossils aged from 1.8 million to 400,000 years; it gave its name to the Oldowan.

kilwa-kisiwani.fait: This island very close to the coast had more than 10,000 inhabitants at its peak in the Middle Ages; today it is home to fewer than 1,000.

ravitoto.fait: The name of this recipe means “pounded cassava leaves”: they are cooked with garlic and served with pork or zebu and rice.

rova.fait: This fortified royal enclosure overlooks the capital from the hill of Analamanga; the word “rova” means a royal fortress.

nosy-be.fait: Its name means “big island” in Malagasy; located in the Mozambique Channel, it has become a major tourist destination.

fanorona.fait: This abstract strategy board game exists in three categories; Malagasy people play it everywhere, in towns as well as in the countryside.

zuma-rock.fait: This granite monolith rises 300 meters above the surrounding terrain; it is pictured on the 100-naira note.

osun-oshogbo.fait: This 75-hectare “sacred forest” is also an archaeological site, added to the World Heritage List in 2005.

eyo.fait: This Yoruba masquerade unique to Lagos, also called the Adamu Orisa Play, is traditionally celebrated on Lagos Island.

adire.fait: This indigo-dyed cloth is made by Yoruba women in the southwest of the country; its name means “tie and dye.”

udu.fait: The name of this percussion instrument means “jar” in the Igbo language, after its shape; it is a cousin of the ghatam of India.

attieke.fait: This fermented, steamed cassava semolina has a slightly sour taste; it is eaten with fish, meat and vegetables.

alloco.fait: This is the Ivorian name for a plantain-based dish, called “dodo” in Benin or “loco” in Senegal.

koutoukou.fait: This spirit, also called gbêlê, is made by distilling the sap of palm trees such as the oil palm, the raffia palm or the palmyra palm.

grand-bassam.fait: This town was the first capital of Côte d'Ivoire, from 1893 to 1900; its historic heart, the Quartier France, is a World Heritage Site.

mosquee-kong.fait: Destroyed by Samory Touré around 1897, this great mosque in northern Côte d'Ivoire was rebuilt at the dawn of the 20th century.

zaouli.fait: This name refers at once to a mask, a costume and a dance of the Guro people; the best dancers have been timed at more than 200 steps per minute.

palais-abomey.fait: This group of royal palaces houses a history museum; the 47-hectare site has been a World Heritage Site since 1985.

ganvie.fait: This lake village on Lake Nokoué, north of the Cotonou metropolitan area, is nicknamed the Venice of Africa.

temple-pythons.fait: This voodoo sanctuary in Ouidah houses live sacred pythons; a snake cult has been attested there since the late 17th century.

zangbeto.fait: The name of this masked society means “night hunter”: it hunts sorcerers and evil spirits. Its stronghold is in Porto-Novo.

zemidjan.fait: The name of this motorcycle taxi means “take me quickly” in the Fon language; it is widespread throughout West Africa.

evala.fait: These initiation rites of Kabye country, marked mainly by wrestling, take young people aged 18 to 20 into adulthood.

mont-agou.fait: The highest peak in Togo at 986 meters, this mountain covered with dense forests is home to many small Ewe villages.

cathedrale-lome.fait: This cathedral was erected in just over a year, from April 1901 to September 1902, by the German colonial authorities.

ayimolou.fait: This dish of rice and beans cooked together, often sold on the street, is eaten for breakfast as well as for lunch or dinner.

loropeni.fait: These ruins in the South-West Region of Burkina Faso have been on the UNESCO World Heritage List since 2009.

tiebele.fait: This traditional architectural complex, more than 500 years old, has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since July 2024.

dan-fani.fait: The full name of this hand-spun and hand-woven cotton textile, Faso Dan Fani, comes from Dyula and means “woven wrapper of the homeland.”

chapeau-sapone.fait: This traditional braided straw hat, decorated with leather, is called “Sapon pougla” in Mooré; it comes from the rural commune of Saponé.

mosquee-agadez.fait: Built in 1515 with the clay known as “banco” and restored in 1844, it has a 27-meter minaret, the tallest structure in the town.

arbre-tenere.fait: This solitary acacia, once considered the most isolated tree on Earth, served as a landmark for caravans; a truck knocked it down in 1973.

guerewol.fait: During this courtship ritual of the Wodaabe, young men put on makeup, dance and sing to attract the attention of young women.

croix-agadez.fait: This Tuareg pendant, formed of a lozenge topped by a circle, is said to have been created in the Aïr; it is the most famous piece of Tuareg jewelry.

dabous.fait: These rock engravings dated to the Neolithic are found on the western side of the Aïr Mountains, in central Niger.

ndole.fait: This dish bears the Cameroonian name of a leaf vegetable, Vernonia, whose leaves are eaten fresh or, more rarely, dried.

poulet-dg.fait: In this sauté of chicken and plantains, “DG” stands for “directeur général,” managing director: the dish was originally reserved for important people.

chutes-lobe.fait: Seven kilometers south of Kribi, these falls have a rare feature: the Lobé River flows directly into the Atlantic Ocean.

nguon.fait: This cultural event of the Bamum kingdom, made up of rituals and festivities, was established by Nchare Yen one year after the founding of the kingdom, in 1394.

toghu.fait: This royal garment with colorful patterns of the Grassfields peoples was chosen as the traditional outfit at the 2012 London Olympic Games.

virunga.fait: Created in 1925 to protect mountain gorillas, it is the oldest national park in Africa; it was originally called Albert Park.

nyiragongo.fait: This 3,470-meter stratovolcano holds an almost permanent lava lake; its lava flows are considered the fastest in the world.

velours-kasai.fait: This traditional raffia cloth is made by the Kuba in the Kasai region, in the Democratic Republic of the Congo.

lola-ya-bonobo.fait: Its name means “paradise of the bonobos”: this sanctuary south of Kinshasa takes in baby bonobos that are victims of poaching.

parc-volcans.fait: This national park is in northwestern Rwanda, near the town of Ruhengeri, 120 kilometers north of Kigali.

nyungwe.fait: This forest massif in southwestern Rwanda, protected by a national park, covers an area of about 970 km².

akagera.fait: Created in 1934 to protect the animals of the savanna, mountains and swamps, this park takes its name from the Kagera River, which flows through it.

imigongo.fait: The relief of these panels painted with geometric patterns is created with calf dung; this art is traditionally practiced by women.

sossusvlei.fait: This salt and clay pan, surrounded by high red sand dunes, is the most visited tourist site in Namibia.

fish-river-canyon.fait: At 160 km long, this canyon is the largest in Africa and one of the largest in the world; it reaches a depth of 550 meters.

etosha.fait: Created in 1907 as a game reserve, this protected area is home to 114 species of mammals; the public has access to only about a third of the park.

kolmanskop.fait: Once a thriving diamond-mining site, this ghost town near Lüderitz is being invaded by sand from the Namib Desert.

hoba.fait: At 60 metric tons in a single piece, it is the largest known meteorite and the largest known natural block of iron on the Earth's surface.

otjize.fait: This cosmetic paste of the OvaHimba, made of red ocher mixed with fat or clarified butter, gives the skin and hair a red tint.

okavango.fait: It is the second-largest inland delta in the world: with no outlet to the sea, its waters coming from Angola spill into the Kalahari Desert.

chobe.fait: The first national park in Botswana, it is known for its lions that hunt African elephants, often young ones but sometimes adults.

tsodilo.fait: With nearly 4,500 rock paintings over about 10 km² in the Kalahari Desert, this site is sometimes nicknamed the “Louvre of the Desert.”

seswaa.fait: This dish of boiled then pounded meat, most often beef, is traditionally prepared by men for major celebrations.

mokoro.fait: This dugout canoe about 6 meters long is maneuvered standing at the stern, pushing with a long pole in the shallow waters of the delta.

kgotla.fait: In this traditional public assembly, usually in the center of the village, everyone has the right to speak without being interrupted, and discussions must reach a consensus.

cachupa.fait: Considered a national dish, this stew has corn and dried beans as its basic ingredients.

grogue.fait: This sugarcane spirit, with an alcohol content of around 40%, is related to rhum agricole; it is the national drink of Cape Verde.

pico-do-fogo.fait: The highest point in the country at 2,829 meters, this active volcano is also the highest peak in West Africa.

cidade-velha.fait: The first colonial town built by Europeans in the tropics, it was once the capital of Cape Verde; it was originally called Ribeira Grande.

carnaval-mindelo.fait: This annual festival takes place on an island of Cape Verde, of which it is a symbol of identity, as Cesária Évora says in a song.

morne-brabant.fait: This mountain in the southwest of the island was a refuge for runaway slaves; today it is a place of remembrance of the colonial period.

sept-couleurs.fait: This geological formation, now a tourist attraction, is located in Chamarel, in the Black River district.

aapravasi-ghat.fait: It was here, in the Port Louis district, that Indian indentured laborers arriving on the island landed, from November 1834 to 1910.

pamplemousses.fait: Created by Pierre Poivre, it is the first tropical botanical garden in the world; it succeeded a garden founded in 1735 to supply ships.

coco-de-mer.fait: This palm produces the largest seed in the world, nicknamed “cocofesse,” which can weigh around twenty kilograms.

vallee-de-mai.fait: On the island of Praslin, this reserve, listed as a World Heritage Site in 1983, is home to one of the largest forests of coco de mer palms.

anse-source-argent.fait: This 2-km beach on the island of La Digue is famous for its white sand, its clusters of granite boulders and its shallow turquoise waters.

la-digue.fait: The fourth-largest island in the archipelago, it lives off tourism thanks to its fine white sand beaches, including the famous Anse Source d'Argent.

moutya.fait: This traditional dance is performed around a fire to the sound of a drum; once practiced by slaves, it has been inscribed by UNESCO since 2021.

guelta-archei.fait: In a remote part of this guelta on the Ennedi Plateau survives a completely isolated population of desert crocodiles.

zakouma.fait: Created in 1963 in southeastern Chad, this national park is managed by the NGO African Parks, which combines tourism and wildlife conservation there.

toumai.fait: This fossil skull about 7 million years old, discovered in 2001 in the Djurab Desert, bears a nickname meaning “hope of life.”

bento.fait: This complete individual meal is presented in a compartmentalized box, from simple disposable packaging to a lacquered wooden case.

rio-platano.fait: This region of tropical forests, where 2,000 Indigenous people still live, has been a World Heritage Site since 1982 and listed as in danger since 2011.

yojoa.fait: This lake straddles three departments, 184 km from the capital, Tegucigalpa; it was designated a Ramsar site on May 5, 2005.

cayos-cochinos.fait: This archipelago consists of two small islands and 13 smaller coral cays, 30 km northeast of La Ceiba.

guanaja.fait: Most of its 10,000 inhabitants live in Bonacca, a main town built not on the island itself but on a pair of coral reefs.

pupusa.fait: This thick corn or rice flatbread, stuffed with cheese or beans, has been declared the national dish; it even has a day dedicated to it.

joya-ceren.fait: This archaeological site, 25 km from San Salvador in the department of La Libertad, is nicknamed the “Pompeii of the Americas.”

tazumal.fait: The metal objects found in this Maya complex date from the 8th century and are among the oldest reported in Mesoamerica.

volcan-santa-ana.fait: At 2,381 meters, it is the country's highest volcano; its last eruption, in 2005, hurled ash and rocks over more than a kilometer.

coatepeque.fait: This lake fills a caldera and is part of the Apaneca-Ilamatepec Biosphere Reserve, recognized by UNESCO in 2007.

granada-ni.fait: Its Andalusian-style buildings earned it the nickname “Great Sultana”; this city stretches along Lake Nicaragua, overlooked by the Mombacho volcano.

cathedrale-leon-ni.nom: Cathedral of the Assumption of León
cathedrale-leon-ni.fait: Built from 1747 to 1814, this Baroque cathedral has withstood earthquakes and volcanic eruptions thanks to the sturdiness of its walls.

volcan-masaya.fait: It is one of the few volcanoes in the world where you can drive right up to the edge of the crater; it is only 25 km from Managua.

gueguense.fait: This satirical theatrical tradition combines masked street theater, music and folk ballet; it is also spelled “Güegüence.”

iles-mais.fait: These two islands in the Caribbean Sea, Big and Little, lie about 75 km off the coast; they are most often called the Corn Islands.

arenal.fait: The youngest volcano in the country, this almost symmetrical cone remained in eruption from July 29, 1968, to December 2010.

spheres-diquis.fait: Several hundred of these stone balls have been discovered in the south of the country; they are commonly attributed to the ancient Diquís culture.

corcovado-cr.fait: Established in 1975 on the Osa Peninsula, this park was described by National Geographic as the most intense place in the world in terms of biodiversity.

ile-cocos.fait: Lying 491 km off the coast, this volcanic island in the Pacific is known for having hosted pirates who hid their treasures there.

monteverde.fait: This reserve protects about 10,500 hectares of tropical cloud forest on the foothills of the Cordillera de Tilarán.

manuel-antonio.fait: Established in 1972 on the Pacific coast, this park covers 1,983 hectares of land and 55,000 of sea; in 2011, Forbes ranked it among the 12 most beautiful in the world.

canal-panama.nom: Canal linking the Atlantic and the Pacific
canal-panama.fait: At 80 km long, it opened on August 15, 1914: from New York to San Francisco, it cuts the journey from 22,500 to 9,500 kilometers.

san-blas.fait: This coastal archipelago in the Caribbean Sea, sometimes called the Mulatas Archipelago, is administratively part of the comarca of Guna Yala.

mola.fait: Kuna women sew together several layers of fabric in different colors, then cut them with scissors to reveal designs.

fort-san-lorenzo.fait: This ruined fort overlooks the mouth of the Chagres River; it was part of the Spanish Crown's defense system for transatlantic trade.

bocas-del-toro.fait: The main town of this Caribbean archipelago is Bocas del Toro, on Colón Island; all its islands can be reached by water taxi.

citadelle-ferriere.fait: Built in the early 19th century by Henri Christophe, it is the largest fortress in the Americas; it could hold up to 5,000 men.

sans-souci.fait: This palace in Milot, in the north of the country, was the main residence of Henri Christophe; it lies about twenty kilometers from Cap-Haïtien.

tap-tap.fait: These shared taxis are the country's main means of transportation, including in its capital, Port-au-Prince.

soupe-joumou.fait: This pumpkin soup has been on the list of the Intangible Cultural Heritage of Humanity since December 16, 2021.

rara.fait: This musical form originating in Haiti is played during street parades, usually during Easter week.

compas.fait: Created in the mid-1950s by saxophonist Nemours Jean-Baptiste, this genre borrows elements from jazz and Cuban music.

carnaval-jacmel.fait: Celebrated since 1991 on the Sunday before the national carnival, it showcases local culture, including giant papier-mâché masks.

marche-fer.fait: Also called the Hyppolite Market or the Vallières Market, it is the best known of the public markets in Port-au-Prince, the capital.

pikliz.fait: This condiment combines shredded carrots and white cabbage, onions and chili peppers, seasoned with lime juice or vinegar; it is served with pressed fried plantains.

bachata.fait: Initially scorned because it came from the lower social classes, this guitar music began to gain popularity in the 1980s.

zone-coloniale-sd.fait: This historic heart of the capital, called “Zona Colonial” in Spanish, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

cathedrale-primatiale.fait: Built in the early 16th century by the Spanish in Santo Domingo, it is the first cathedral constructed on the American continent.

punta-cana.fait: At the country's eastern tip, this town of about 50,000 inhabitants is its main beach resort.

forteresse-ozama.fait: Built between 1502 and 1505, it is one of the first European military structures in the Americas; it served as a prison until the 1960s.

larimar.fait: This gemstone, a variety of pectolite, is found in the Dominican Republic; its color ranges from white to dark blue.

trou-bleu-dean.fait: At 202 meters deep, this blue hole was the deepest in the world before the discovery of the Dragon Hole in the South China Sea.

exumas.fait: This archipelago of more than 360 islands or islets stretches over more than 200 kilometers; the Tropic of Cancer runs through George Town, on the island of Great Exuma.

bimini-road.fait: Some have seen it as a remnant of Atlantis; to geologists, these underwater stones are beach deposits hardened by natural processes.

eleuthera.fait: Very elongated, this island is 180 km long and barely 2 km wide; its name comes from a Greek word meaning “free.”

pig-beach.fait: This uninhabited island in the Exumas is home to many released pigs, which root around the beaches at low tide and even go into the water.

steel-drum.fait: This melodic percussion instrument is played in orchestras called “steelbands”; their rehearsal space is known as a “panyard.”

calypso.fait: Also called “kaiso,” this musical genre closely tied to carnival has spread to the rest of the Caribbean and to Venezuela.

carnaval-tt.fait: This festival takes place on the Monday and Tuesday before Ash Wednesday; since the '70s, soca has been the music most played in the streets.

lac-brea.fait: This natural asphalt lake, one of the largest in the world, covers about 40 hectares and reaches 75 meters at its deepest point.

pitons.fait: These volcanic spires are the emblem of Saint Lucia; they appear, in stylized form, on the national flag.

qualibou.fait: Also called Soufrière, this volcano in Saint Lucia consists of a caldera partly submerged by the Caribbean Sea.

mont-gimie.fait: The highest mountain in Saint Lucia at 950 m, this peak of volcanic origin can only be climbed with an accredited local guide.

cathedrale-castries.nom: Cathedral of the Immaculate Conception, Castries
cathedrale-castries.fait: This large Catholic building in Castries, Saint Lucia, is both a basilica and a cathedral; it is the seat of the Archdiocese of Castries.

pain-de-sucre.fait: This 396-meter granite monolith rises at the mouth of Guanabara Bay in Rio de Janeiro; it is reached by cable car.

copacabana.fait: Stretching 4.5 km, this Rio de Janeiro beach is nicknamed the “Princess of the Sea” and is considered one of the most famous in the world.

ouro-preto.fait: Born from the discovery of gold in the rivers of Minas Gerais, this town founded in 1711 had more inhabitants around 1750 than Rio de Janeiro or New York.

rencontre-eaux.fait: Near Manaus, the ocher waters of the Solimões River and the black waters of the Rio Negro flow side by side without mixing for dozens of kilometers.

brigadeiro.fait: This Brazilian chocolate confection has uncertain origins: depending on the source, it dates back to the 1940s or to the 19th century.

pao-de-queijo.fait: This “cheese bread” is typical of the Brazilian states of Minas Gerais and Goiás; it is also found in Paraguay under the name chipa.

acaraje.fait: These small balls of black-eyed pea dough, onion and salt are fried in palm oil; they are an Afro-Brazilian culinary specialty.

moqueca.fait: This fish stew with tomatoes, onions, peppers and cilantro simmers slowly in a clay pot; it is typical of Bahia, Pará and Espírito Santo.

coxinha.fait: Its name means “little chicken thigh”: chopped or shredded chicken, covered in dough, shaped like a teardrop, then breaded and fried.

caipirinha.fait: This Brazilian cocktail combines cachaça, sugar and lime; it is said to have been created by peasants, hence its name, which means “little country girl.”

cachaca.fait: This Brazilian spirit is made from fresh sugarcane juice, fermented and then distilled; it is older than rum.

pandeiro.fait: A Brazilian version of the tambourine, this percussion instrument was brought to Brazil by the first Portuguese colonizers.

tamborim.fait: This Brazilian percussion instrument is a modern small frame drum; it is very different from the pandeiro.

samba.fait: This genre of music and dance was born in the early 20th century in the Afro-Brazilian communities of Rio de Janeiro; its dancers are called sambistas.

frevo.fait: This word refers to both a carnival music and a dance from Recife, capital of the state of Pernambuco, in northeastern Brazil.

maracatu.fait: This carnival procession from Pernambuco, Brazil, is rooted in the history of enslaved people and in ceremonies crowning Kongo kings and queens.

ecole-samba.fait: Originating in Rio de Janeiro, these groups parade in costume around a theme, with several hundred or even a few thousand people.

bumba-meu-boi.fait: This Brazilian folk dance brings together human characters and fantastic animals around the death and resurrection of an ox.

festival-parintins.fait: This popular festival is held every year on the last weekend of June in Parintins, in the Amazon region of Brazil.

cirio-nazare.fait: This Catholic festival in northern Brazil draws more than two million people every year to the city of Belém, in the state of Pará.

jangada.fait: This Portuguese word refers both to a wooden raft drifting down a river and to a traditional boat used by fishermen along the Brazilian coast.

aconcagua.fait: At 6,962 meters, this peak located thirteen kilometers from the Chilean border is the highest mountain outside Asia.

humahuaca.fait: This deep canyon in Jujuy Province, in northwestern Argentina, is home to villages rich in pre-Columbian and colonial remains.

ushuaia.fait: This capital of Tierra del Fuego Province is considered the southernmost city in the world; its port is one of the closest to Antarctica.

casa-rosada.fait: This seat of Argentina's executive branch, in central Buenos Aires, owes its name to the pink color of its facades; the president has an office there.

theatre-colon.fait: This Buenos Aires opera house is considered one of the best in the world for its size, its acoustics and its history.

ischigualasto.fait: Also called Valle de la Luna, this 63,000-hectare provincial park lies in the far northeast of San Juan Province, Argentina.

san-ignacio-mini.fait: These ruins in Misiones Province are those of a Jesuit mission founded in the early 17th century to evangelize the Guarani.

cafe-tortoni.fait: Opened in 1858 in Buenos Aires by a French Basque immigrant, this café is named after a Parisian establishment on the Boulevard des Italiens.

chimichurri.fait: This chili-based condiment, originally from Argentina, is a variant of green sauce, although a red version also exists.

choripan.fait: This sandwich combines a sausage and a bread roll, sometimes seasoned with chimichurri; in Argentina, it is eaten at an asado or as fast food.

pato.fait: This equestrian sport born among the gauchos was originally played with a dead bird, usually a duck, inside a leather bag; it is Argentina's national sport.

chacarera.fait: This couple dance from northern Argentina is characterized by its triple rhythm and the use of string instruments and the bombo legüero.

malambo.fait: This Argentine folk dance is performed solo; created in the 17th century in the Pampas, it is accompanied by a drum called a bombo and by guitars.

fileteado.fait: Born in Buenos Aires toward the end of the 19th century, this style of decorative painting originally adorned animal-drawn freight carts.

eglises-chiloe.fait: These wooden churches from the 17th and 18th centuries blend European Jesuit culture with the traditions and techniques of the archipelago's local peoples.

cap-horn.fait: Located in the Chilean part of Tierra del Fuego, this cape with strong and frequent storms has a reputation as a graveyard of ships.

la-moneda.fait: Its name means “Palace of the Mint”; located in Santiago, this building is the seat of the presidency of Chile.

humberstone.nom: Humberstone and Santa Laura Saltpeter Works
humberstone.fait: These two former sites in the Tarapacá Region, in northern Chile, were used to process potassium nitrate.

detroit-magellan.fait: At 611 kilometers long, this natural passage between the Atlantic and the Pacific is named after the first European to cross it, in 1520.

curanto.fait: This dish from the Chiloé archipelago is traditionally prepared in a hole about a meter and a half deep, on red-hot stones.

completo.fait: This Chilean version of the hot dog, bigger than the American one, is topped, depending on the variant, with avocado, tomato, mayonnaise or sauerkraut.

mote-huesillo.fait: This nonalcoholic drink made with cooked wheat and dried peach inspired the expression “more Chilean than mote con huesillo.”

chorrillana.fait: This dish of Chilean cuisine is a plate of French fries topped with various meats, eggs or fried onions.

rodeo-huaso.fait: The second most popular sport in Chile after soccer, it is practiced by pairs of huasos on horseback who must stop a bull.

rongo-rongo.fait: These signs carved in wood, discovered on Easter Island, have resisted every attempt at decipherment; they may constitute a script.

sacsayhuaman.fait: This Inca fortress at 3,700 m above sea level, two kilometers from Cusco, is shaped like the head of a puma, a sacred animal in Inca tradition.

ollantaytambo.fait: The name of this Inca fortress means “Ollantay's inn,” after a warrior; Manco Inca took refuge there after the fall of Cusco.

moray.fait: These Inca terraces in concentric circles create some twenty microclimates; they may have been an ancient agricultural research center.

chan-chan.fait: Capital of the Chimor empire from 900 to 1470, this site near Trujillo was the largest city of the pre-Columbian era in South America.

kuelap.fait: This fortress was built in the 10th century by the Chachapoyas on a ridge overlooking the Utcubamba Valley, in northern Peru.

colca.fait: At 3,270 m deep, this canyon was once thought to be the deepest in the world; from a natural lookout, condors can be seen soaring.

caral.fait: This archaeological site, in the desert 23 km from the coast of Peru, is the remnant of the oldest known city in the Americas to date.

santa-catalina.fait: This convent in Arequipa, which covers 2 hectares, is home to a community of Dominican nuns; it is presented as the largest in the world.

huacachina.fait: This village near Ica is built around a small lake; according to legend, a princess turned mermaid still swims in its waters.

lomo-saltado.fait: This sliced beef stir-fry appeared around the mid-19th century under the influence of Cantonese Chinese immigrants; it is cooked in a wok with soy sauce.

aji-gallina.fait: Its name means “hen with chili pepper”; this dish from Lima, with Spanish and French influences, is widespread throughout Peru.

anticucho.fait: In Peru, these skewers are notably made with pieces of beef heart, marinated and then grilled; they are also eaten in Bolivia and Chile.

pachamanca.fait: This Peruvian specialty is cooked underground with hot stones; it is usually prepared for gatherings.

picarones.fait: These fritters made from squash and sweet potato, originally from Lima, are covered in chancaca, a kind of solid molasses.

chicha-morada.fait: This nonalcoholic drink is made from purple corn, a Peruvian variety; depending on the season, it is drunk hot or well chilled.

inti-raymi.fait: This “festival of the sun” of Inca origin honors the winter solstice; it is held on June 24 at the fortress of Sacsayhuamán, near Cusco.

qoyllur-riti.fait: This pilgrimage brings together about 90,000 people from the Cusco region every year; its high point is a night walk to the top of a glacier.

quipu.fait: Lacking writing, the Inca administration recorded numbers with knots on cords of various colors attached to a main rope.

tumi.fait: This knife with a semicircular blade was used for sacrifices before the Spanish conquest; in Peru, hanging one on the wall is believed to bring good luck.

ciudad-perdida.fait: This ancient city in the Sierra Nevada de Santa Marta is believed to have been founded around 800 AD, 650 years earlier than Machu Picchu.

san-agustin.fait: This park in the Andes has 300 monumental sculptures, left by a culture that reached its peak during the first eight centuries of the Common Era.

las-lajas.fait: This Catholic sanctuary in the canyon of the Guáitara River, 7 km from Ipiales, has been a major pilgrimage center since the 18th century.

penon-guatape.fait: This 220-meter-high monolith, also called Piedra del Peñol, rises in Guatapé, in the department of Antioquia, Colombia.

monserrate.fait: This hill bordering Bogotá to the east was called “cerro de las Nieves,” the Hill of the Snows, until the mid-17th century.

villa-de-leyva.fait: This small colonial town in the department of Boyacá is known for its huge cobblestone main square; a kite festival is held there in mid-August.

san-felipe-barajas.fait: This fort in Cartagena de Indias is the largest fortress built by the Spanish during their colonial period; the first fort dates from 1536.

tayrona.fait: This protected area in the Caribbean region, 34 km from Santa Marta, includes 150 km² of land and 30 km² of marine area.

bandeja-paisa.fait: This typical dish of Antioquian cuisine stands out for its abundance and variety; served in full, it comes only on a platter.

lechona.fait: This typical dish of the Tolima region consists of pieces of suckling pig and peas; it is served with insulso, a corn-based dough.

tejo.fait: This traditional sport, also called turmequé, originated with the Chibcha Indigenous people in west-central Colombia.

sombrero-vueltiao.fait: This hat made of arrow cane has its origins in the Indigenous Zenú culture; in 2004, the Colombian Congress declared it a cultural symbol of the nation.

carnaval-barranquilla.fait: This 19th-century tradition begins on the Saturday before Ash Wednesday and ends on Mardi Gras; thousands of people take part.

noirs-et-blancs.fait: This carnival in San Juan de Pasto takes place from December 28 to January 7, outside the usual calendar of carnivals around Mardi Gras.

velitas.fait: On the night of December 7, Colombians light lanterns and candles in the streets to celebrate the Immaculate Conception.

poporo.fait: Among certain ethnic groups such as the Kogi, this gourd is given to a young boy to mark his passage from child to adult of marrying age.

salar-uyuni.fait: This salt desert stretches across the high plateaus of southwestern Bolivia; it takes its name from the nearby town of Uyuni.

laguna-colorada.fait: This salt lake on the Bolivian Altiplano, at an altitude of 4,278 m, covers 60 km² with an average depth of 35 centimeters.

isla-del-sol.fait: The largest island in Lake Titicaca, it was originally called Isla Titikaka: it is the island that gave the great lake its name.

cerro-rico.fait: Mined for its mineral resources since the 16th century, this 4,782 m peak towers over Potosí; its profile appears on the coat of arms of Bolivia.

route-yungas.fait: Very narrow, without guardrails and often shrouded in fog, this road from 1930 linking La Paz to Coroico was nicknamed the “Road of Death.”

marche-sorcieres.fait: In downtown La Paz, this market sells ritual objects from Aymara culture; magic rites are also performed there.

chiquitos.fait: These settlements founded by the Jesuits in the 17th and 18th centuries are located in the north of the department of Santa Cruz, Bolivia.

carnaval-oruro.fait: The largest annual cultural event in Bolivia, this carnival is part of the Ito festival, celebrated in honor of the Uru people.

ekeko.fait: This Aymara god of abundance, fertility and happiness remains present in Bolivia in the form of a figurine called an equeco.

alasitas.fait: Starting on January 24 in La Paz, people buy a miniature of a dream they wish to fulfill there, then offer it to Ekeko, the Aymara god of abundance.

saltena.fait: This baked empanada contains broth, meat, hard-boiled egg and spices; in Bolivia, it is eaten mostly in the morning.

api.fait: This drink from the Andean Altiplano owes its purple color to purple corn; its Quechua name refers to a preparation made from corn flour.

pique-macho.fait: This dish of beef, French fries, onions and hard-boiled eggs is said to have been born in the 1970s at the El Prado restaurant in Cochabamba.

silpancho.fait: Its Quechua name means “flat and thin”: a round piece of breaded, fried beef covers the plate in this dish from Cochabamba.

galapagos.fait: This archipelago of some forty volcanic islands has been a province of Ecuador since 1832; the easternmost one is 929 km from the mainland.

cotopaxi.fait: The highest active volcano in Ecuador at 5,897 meters, this perfect cone destroyed several towns during its 1877 eruption.

chimborazo.fait: The highest summit in the Ecuadorian Andes at 6,263 m, this volcano is nicknamed Taita Chimborazo, meaning “Papa Chimborazo.”

quilotoa.fait: The volcano in Ecuador that bears this name rises to 3,914 m, about thirty kilometers west of Latacunga, in the south of the Cordillera Occidental.

ingapirca.fait: The name of this archaeological complex in Cañar Province, Ecuador, means “Inca wall” in the Kichwa language.

compania-quito.fait: This 17th-century Jesuit church, in the historic center of Quito, is considered one of the seven wonders of Ecuador.

basilique-voeu.fait: Dedicated to the Sacred Heart, this basilica is the largest neo-Gothic building in Latin America; its towers are the tallest structures in Quito.

panama-chapeau.fait: Despite its name, this hat is of Ecuadorian origin; it is handmade from the leaves of a plant, Carludovica palmata.

encebollado.fait: This fish dish from Ecuador's Pacific coast is cooked with yuca, red onions and lime in a tomato broth.

fanesca.fait: This soup is prepared the week before Easter with twelve grains from the Ecuadorian Andes, each representing a disciple of Jesus.

llapingacho.fait: These mashed potato patties with melted cheese are a popular and very inexpensive dish in Ecuador, served as a side.

colada-morada.fait: This thick purple drink is made in Ecuador with fruits typical of the country, spices and corn flour.

rondador.fait: This set of reed panpipes produces two sounds at once; it is considered the national instrument of Ecuador.

salto-angel.fait: At 807 m, this waterfall has the highest drop in the world; it is named after Jimmy Angel, an American aviator who flew over the site in 1933.

canaima.fait: Created on June 12, 1962 on the Guiana Shield, in the state of Bolívar, this park has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1994.

auyan-tepuy.fait: Its Arekuna name means “devil's mountain”; this plateau of nearly 700 km² towers nearly 1,000 meters above the forest of the Gran Sabana.

los-roques.fait: This archipelago of about 350 islands, cays or islets lies about 130 km off the coast of Venezuela and has 1,500 inhabitants.

catatumbo.fait: This storm occurs 140 to 160 nights a year above the mouth of the Catatumbo River, with a frequency of 280 lightning strikes per hour.

hallaca.fait: This Venezuelan Christmas dish is a corn dough usually filled with meat, olives and raisins, boiled in a banana leaf.

cachapa.fait: This thick pancake of fresh yellow corn, worked with milk and sugar, comes from Venezuela; it is often served with fresh cheese.

tequeno.fait: According to popular belief, these sticks of hard white cheese wrapped in a strip of dough and then fried owe their name to the town of Los Teques, their place of origin.

diables-yare.fait: On the ninth Thursday after Holy Thursday, dancers in red costumes and demon masks represent the triumph of good over evil.

liqui-liqui.fait: This outfit from the Llanos region is a Creole adaptation of clothing from the Philippines; it has been the national costume of Venezuela since 2017.

colonia-sacramento.fait: Capital of the department of Colonia, in southwestern Uruguay, this town is also the oldest in the country.

stade-centenario.fait: Located in the Parque Batlle neighborhood of Montevideo, this stadium, used mainly for soccer, commemorates the centenary of Uruguay's independence.

theatre-solis.fait: Opened in 1856 in the Old Town of Montevideo, this theater is considered the oldest in South America.

cabo-polonio.fait: This hamlet in the department of Rocha, Uruguay, is both a beach resort and a national and natural park.

punta-del-este.fait: This beach resort on Maldonado Bay stands out for its two large beaches, Playa Mansa and Playa Brava, which contribute greatly to its reputation.

palais-legislatif-uy.fait: This palace is the seat of the General Assembly of Uruguay, a parliament made up of the Chamber of Representatives and the Senate.

candombe.fait: This musical genre emerged in Uruguay; according to some musicologists, it has its origins in the rhythms of Bantu Africa.

chivito.fait: This meat sandwich, typical of Uruguay, is usually served with mayonnaise, French fries and Olivier salad.

palacio-lopez.fait: This neoclassical palace, on the bank of the Paraguay River in central Asunción, houses the seat of the presidency of the Republic.

tavarangue.fait: These ruins in the department of Itapúa are those of one of the thirty reductions founded by the Jesuits for the Guarani people.

terere.fait: Similar to mate but drunk cold, with lots of ice and often medicinal herbs, this beverage originated in Paraguay.

chipa.fait: This food, traditionally made from cassava starch and cheese, comes in about 70 varieties in Paraguay, where a national day is dedicated to it on August 9.

fort-zeelandia.fait: This pentagon-shaped fort, built by the Dutch in Paramaribo to protect a trading post, has become a museum.

jodensavanne.fait: This name referred to a Jewish settlement on the banks of the Suriname River, about 50 km south of Paramaribo, that grew sugarcane.

palais-presidentiel-sr.fait: Facing Independence Square, this palace is one of the best-maintained examples of Dutch colonial architecture in Suriname.

neve-shalom.fait: Completed in 1842, it is the only synagogue in Suriname; in Paramaribo, it stands next to the city's main mosque.

keti-koti.fait: Every July 1, this holiday celebrates the abolition of slavery; its name, in Sranan Tongo, literally means “broken chains.”

caacupe.fait: This church in Caacupé, Paraguay, is at once a cathedral, a minor basilica and a national shrine for the Catholic Church.
